Recalibrate forecast distributions on recent years

Source: R/model-recalibrate.R
recalibrated.Rd

Wraps any model specification so that its forecast distribution is recalibrated on the last years observed years of the training data: the spread (and optionally the trend) of its draws is rescaled (method = "spread", default), or the draws are replaced by the point forecast of the model plus resampled errors of its past forecasts (method = "errors"). Each time the model is fitted (also at every origin of an outer mt_backtest()):

Usage

recalibrated(
  spec,
  years = 10,
  n_origins = 5,
  scale = c("constant", "horizon", "per_horizon"),
  bias = FALSE,
  target = c("crps", "interval"),
  level = 0.95,
  by = NULL,
  n_draws = 100,
  seed = 1,
  ages = NULL,
  quantity = c("rate", "life_expectancy", "asr"),
  n_boot = 0,
  method = c("spread", "errors")
)

Arguments

spec

A model specification.

years

Length of the calibration window (the last observed years).

n_origins

Number of origins in the window (evenly spaced from years to 2 years before the end of the training data; at most years - 1). The per-horizon methods need two origins at each forecast horizon (see "Factors per horizon").

scale

"constant" (default: one spread factor \(s_1\) for all horizons), "per_horizon" (one factor for each horizon) or the deprecated "horizon" (spread factor \(s_1 h^{\gamma}\), package-specific; use "per_horizon").

bias

Estimate a correction of the drift (log rate per year; package-specific; with scale = "per_horizon" one for each horizon).

target

"crps" or "interval" (interval score at level).

level

Level of the central interval for target = "interval", and of the interval whose coverage of the inner errors is tuned with method = "errors".

by

Stratum variables with separate calibration parameters.

n_draws

Draws per inner forecast.

seed

Random seed of the inner forecasts and of the simulated observation noise.

ages

Break points between age bands with their own factors (NULL: one set for all ages).

quantity

What is scored: "rate" (log death rates of the observed cells), "life_expectancy" (at birth) or "asr".

n_boot

Number of bootstrap refits for intervals of the factors (0: none; each refit repeats the optimisation, not the inner forecasts).

method

"spread" (default: rescale the spread of the draws) or "errors" (point forecast plus resampled errors of the inner forecasts; see "Resampled past errors"). method = "errors" takes years, n_origins, level, n_draws and seed; the other arguments keep their defaults.

Value

A model specification. The fitted object has a calibration element: a data.table with one row per group and age band (scale_h1, slope, drift, the number of observed cells and of scored values, the number of inner forecasts (stratum x origin), CRPS and coverage of the inner forecasts before and after calibration, and with n_boot the intervals scale_h1_lo, scale_h1_hi, ...). With scale = "per_horizon" it has one row per group, age band and horizon, with horizon, origins (inner origins of the horizon), scale and drift in place of scale_h1, slope and drift (and scale_lo, scale_hi, ... with n_boot). With method = "errors" it has one row per horizon: horizon, origins (error vectors), cells (ages x strata of each vector), mean_error, tuning (\(\pi_h\)) and coverage (share of the inner errors within the tuned interval). For the per-horizon methods, calibration_hmax is the longest horizon that forecasts can reach.

Details

  1. the base model is refitted at n_origins origins inside the calibration window (training data up to the origin) and forecasts the remaining years of the window;

  2. the draws are transformed per cell on the log scale, $$\log m^* = \tilde m + b\,h + s(h)\,(\log m - \tilde m),$$ where \(\tilde m\) is the median of the draws in the cell, \(h\) the horizon, \(s(h)\) a spread factor, one value \(s_1\) for all horizons (scale = "constant", default) or \(s_1 h^{\gamma}\) (scale = "horizon", deprecated), held constant beyond the longest horizon of the window, or one value \(s_h\) for each horizon (scale = "per_horizon"), and \(b\) a correction of the drift per year (bias = TRUE; with scale = "per_horizon" one \(b_h\) for each horizon);

  3. the parameters minimise the mean CRPS (or the interval score, target) of the log death rates in the window, with the Poisson (or the model's negative binomial) variation of the observed deaths, as in mt_backtest(). Draws of an ensemble get the observation noise of the component they come from.

The final model is fitted on all training data and its forecasts are transformed with the estimated parameters. Ranks within each cell are kept, so paths stay paths, and derived quantities such as life expectancy can be computed from the calibrated draws.

Published methods. The closest published method is the member-by-member post-processing of ensemble forecasts (Van Schaeybroeck and Vannitsem 2015), which shifts every member of an ensemble and rescales its deviation from the ensemble mean, with parameters for each lead time estimated by maximum likelihood or minimum CRPS. Here each simulated path is rescaled around the median of the draws of each cell, on the log scale, with one spread factor for all horizons (scale = "constant") estimated by minimum CRPS on inner rolling-origin forecasts. Minimum-CRPS estimation follows ensemble model output statistics (EMOS, Gneiting et al. 2005), which fits a parametric predictive distribution instead of transforming the draws.

Factors per horizon (scale = "per_horizon"). The published post-processing methods fit their parameters to the forecasts of one lead time: Gneiting et al. (2005) fit EMOS to 48-hour forecasts (section 3) and note that distinct forecast horizons may need distinct training periods (section 3a), and member-by-member post-processing is done for each lead time, location and variable separately (Van Schaeybroeck and Vannitsem 2015). The factor \(s_h\) minimises the mean CRPS (or the interval score) of the inner forecasts of horizon \(h\) alone, by the minimum-CRPS estimation of the constant factor (Gneiting et al. 2005, section 2c); with bias = TRUE each horizon also gets its own shift \(b_h h\). Where the spread of the model is wrong by the same factor at every horizon, the factors of all horizons estimate the constant factor, each from fewer forecasts.

The factor of horizon \(h\) rests on the inner origins at least \(h\) years before the last training year. A horizon gets a factor only where at least two origins reach it: the forecast of one origin has the errors of a single year, which all its ages and strata share. When every origin has enough training years, the longest horizon with a factor is years - floor(years / n_origins) (8 with the defaults). The fit reports it as calibration_hmax, and the number of origins of each horizon in column origins. A forecast further ahead stops with an error of class mt_error_recalibrate: no factor is extrapolated. For forecasts of \(h\) years, use for example years = h + 1 and n_origins = h (an origin in every year from \(h + 1\) to 2 years before the last training year); horizon \(h\) then rests on two origins and horizon 1 on \(h\).

Resampled past errors (method = "errors"). The draws are the point forecast of the base model plus errors of its own past forecasts. The inner forecasts are those of step 1, so each inner fit sees the data up to its origin only. The error vector \(e_{o,h}\) of origin \(o\) and horizon \(h\) holds the observed log rates of year \(o + h\) minus the median of the inner draws, for every age of the grid and every stratum. Draw \(j\) of the forecast at horizon \(h\) is $$\log m^*_j = \tilde m + \pi_h\, e_{o_j,h},$$ where \(\tilde m\) is the median of the draws of the base model in the cell (its point forecast) and the origin \(o_j\) is drawn with replacement from the inner origins that reach horizon \(h\), for each draw and horizon.

  • Keilman, Pham and Hetland (2002, section 2) describe the extrapolation of errors of past forecasts: a deterministic forecast gives the expected value, and the errors of historical forecasts give the distribution around it, which they summarise for each forecast duration (section 3.1.1.2).

  • Shang and Hyndman (2017, section 4.4 of the preprint, pointwise intervals) build intervals from h-step errors, observed minus forecast values, resampled with replacement: lower and upper bounds from the resampled errors of each cell are scaled by a tuning factor \(\pi_h\), the one with which a share level of all errors of the horizon lies within the scaled bounds. Here the bounds are the quantiles at \((1 - level) / 2\) and \((1 + level) / 2\) of the bootstrap distribution itself (the empirical distribution of the errors of the cell, the limit of many resamples), and \(\pi_h\) is the smallest such factor. These bounds contain a share level of the errors of each cell, so \(\pi_h \le 1\); with fewer than \(1 / (1 - level)\) origins at a horizon (20 at 95%), they are the smallest and the largest error and \(\pi_h = 1\).

  • One origin per draw and horizon gives all ages and strata the errors of the same past forecast, which keeps their dependence: the joint bootstrap of Panagiotelis et al. (2023).

  • The errors are used as they are, as by Shang and Hyndman (2017), so a mean error of the inner forecasts shifts the forecast distribution away from the point forecast. Keilman, Pham and Hetland (2002, section 2) assume an expected error of zero.

Deviations and package-specific parts (reference unknown): Shang and Hyndman (2017) forecast with principal components estimated from all years; here the model is refitted at each origin, as in the historical forecasts of Keilman, Pham and Hetland (2002). The origins are those of years and n_origins (Shang and Hyndman use every year). The point forecast is the median of the base draws in each cell. The origins are drawn independently for each horizon, so a draw combines the errors of different origins in different years: quantities that combine years, such as cohort measures or deaths summed over years, miss the dependence of the errors over time. Panagiotelis et al. (2023) note that multi-step forecasts need block-wise bootstraps to keep such serial dependence. The errors are those of the observed log rates, with half a death in empty cells as in mt_backtest(), so the draws describe observed rates and predictive draws add nothing. The method needs observed deaths on the age groups of the grid in every cell of the window, and at least two origins at each forecast horizon, as scale = "per_horizon"; otherwise the fit or the forecast stops with an error. The method gives no coverage guarantee: its intervals cover future errors as far as these resemble the errors of the inner forecasts. Keilman, Pham and Hetland (2002) name two limits of past errors: their series are short, and errors may shrink over successive forecast rounds. The draws of a cell at horizon \(h\) lie within \(\pi_h\) times the range of its \(M\) errors. For exchangeable errors, the range of \(M\) errors contains a further one with probability \((M - 1) / (M + 1)\): 0.82 for 10 origins, 0.33 for two. Horizons that few origins reach therefore get narrow intervals; a long years with n_origins = years - 1 gives each horizon more origins.

Package-specific options (reference unknown): the power law of the spread factor over the horizon (scale = "horizon"), the correction of the drift (bias = TRUE), separate factors for age bands (ages) and calibration on life expectancy or the age-standardised rate (quantity). The drift correction and the age bands have published analogues of another form. EMOS corrects the bias of the forecasts in its predictive mean, a linear function of the forecasts with an intercept, estimated together with the spread by minimum CRPS (Gneiting et al. 2005, eq. 10 and section 2c); bias = TRUE shifts the log rates by a drift per year of the horizon, one drift for all horizons (with scale = "per_horizon" one shift per horizon, a bias correction per lead time). Member-by-member post-processing is done for each location separately (Van Schaeybroeck and Vannitsem 2015), and Gneiting et al. (2005, section 3a) note that distinct regions may need distinct training periods; ages estimates separate factors for bands of ages that the user chooses.

Estimation. The parameters are bounded: \(s_1\) (and \(s_h\)) between 0.1 and 20, \(\gamma\) between -1 and 1, and \(b\) between -0.05 and 0.05 (log rate per year). With one parameter (scale = "constant" or, for each horizon, "per_horizon", with bias = FALSE) the log factor is found by stats::optimize() within its bounds; otherwise the parameters are found by Nelder-Mead (stats::optim(), relative tolerance 1e-6, at most 300 iterations), started at \(s_1 = 1\), \(\gamma = 0\), \(b = 0\), with values outside the bounds rejected. The observation noise of the scored forecasts is simulated once (common random numbers), so the score is a deterministic function of the parameters.

Long horizons. The parameters are estimated on horizons 1 to \(h_{max}\), the distance from the first origin to the last training year (10 years with the defaults). With scale = "constant" or "horizon", the spread factor and the drift correction are held at their values at \(h_{max}\) beyond it. A forecast more than twice as long as \(h_{max}\) gives a warning (class mt_warning_recalibrate), because nothing in the training data shows how the spread of the model is wrong at such horizons. With the defaults this concerns forecasts of more than 20 years (mt_forecast() forecasts 10 by default); give a longer years for long projections, or accept the constant factor. The per-horizon methods stop instead (see above).

The wrapper works with any specification, including ensemble(), bootstrapped() and joint models. For reconciled() models the bottom strata are calibrated and the aggregates recomputed from them, so the draws stay coherent. With by, separate parameters are estimated for groups of strata (for example by = "sex"); strata outside these groups (aggregates) use the pooled parameters. Groups with different factors scale the common variation of joint models (such as the common trend of li_lee()) differently, so it no longer cancels in contrasts between the groups, and intervals of gaps between them widen; use pooled parameters when contrasts between the groups are the target.

Calibration needs years more training years than the base model. A spread factor above 1 means that the base model was too narrow in the window; it widens future intervals in proportion. The parameters are estimated from few overlapping forecasts (with the defaults, 5 origins and 30 forecast years, horizons 1 to 10), so they carry their own uncertainty, and they cannot anticipate changes after the window. n_boot refits them on forecasts (stratum x origin) resampled with replacement and reports 95% percentile intervals (with scale = "per_horizon", for each horizon from its forecasts). The inner models are fitted to shorter series than the final model, which matters for models whose uncertainty depends on the length of the series (the drift of a random walk). Compare calibrated and uncalibrated models in an outer backtest.

Age bands (package-specific). With ages (break points, for example c(50, 75)), the factors are estimated separately for each age band, so that a model that is too narrow at old ages and too wide at young ages is corrected at both. Observed cells belong to the band of their lower age; use break points that are bounds of the observed age groups.

Quantity (package-specific). By default the log death rates of single cells are scored. Intervals of life expectancy and ASR also depend on how the ages move together, which the transformation keeps from the base model; quantity = "life_expectancy" (at birth) or "asr" scores these instead, per test year and stratum (fewer scored values, so the factors are less certain).

Tuning and recalibration. recalibrated() keeps the model and its settings and rescales the width of its forecast distribution. Choosing settings (smoothing, number of components, fitting window) by forecast accuracy is tuning, done by tuned() and mt_tune(); the two combine as recalibrated(tuned(...)).

Calibration widens the intervals of models that were too narrow in the recent past and narrows those that were too wide, for example of ensembles whose intervals already covered. With few training years it rests on few forecasts and can make intervals worse; check it in a backtest, as in the vignette "Tuning and recalibration". mt_score_table(by = c("model", "horizon")) gives the coverage of each horizon.

target = "crps" (default) balances calibration and sharpness; target = "interval" minimises the interval score of the central level interval (Gneiting and Raftery 2007), whose optimum is the correct coverage of that interval.

References

Van Schaeybroeck B, Vannitsem S (2015). Ensemble post-processing using member-by-member approaches: theoretical aspects. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 141(688): 807-818. doi:10.1002/qj.2397

Gneiting T, Raftery AE, Westveld AH, Goldman T (2005). Calibrated probabilistic forecasting using ensemble model output statistics and minimum CRPS estimation. Monthly Weather Review 133(5): 1098-1118. doi:10.1175/MWR2904.1

Gneiting T, Raftery AE (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477): 359-378. doi:10.1198/016214506000001437

Keilman N, Pham DQ, Hetland A (2002). Why population forecasts should be probabilistic: illustrated by the case of Norway. Demographic Research 6(15): 409-454. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2002.6.15

Panagiotelis A, Gamakumara P, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2023). Probabilistic forecast reconciliation: properties, evaluation and score optimisation. European Journal of Operational Research 306(2): 693-706. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2022.07.040

Shang HL, Hyndman RJ (2017). Grouped functional time series forecasting: an application to age-specific mortality rates. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics 26(2): 330-343. doi:10.1080/10618600.2016.1237877

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(recalibrated(lee_carter(), years = 8, n_origins = 3, n_draws = 50), x)
fit$calibration
#>     group     band  scale_h1 slope drift cells scored crps_before crps_after
#>    <char>   <char>     <num> <num> <num> <int>  <num>       <num>      <num>
#> 1:    all all ages 0.7630612     0     0  2414   2414  0.03388302 0.03386637
#>    cov80_before cov80_after cov95_before cov95_after forecasts
#>           <num>       <num>        <num>       <num>     <int>
#> 1:    0.7531069   0.7311516    0.8956089   0.8860812         6
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
# one factor per horizon: horizons 1 to 5 rest on at least two origins
fh <- mt_fit(recalibrated(lee_carter(), years = 6, n_origins = 5, n_draws = 50,
                          scale = "per_horizon"), x)
fh$calibration[, c("horizon", "origins", "scale")]
#>    horizon origins     scale
#>      <int>   <int>     <num>
#> 1:       1       5 0.1241023
#> 2:       2       5 0.8355160
#> 3:       3       4 0.1000042
#> 4:       4       3 1.3174286
#> 5:       5       2 0.1005425
# point forecast plus resampled errors of the inner forecasts
fe <- mt_fit(recalibrated(lee_carter(), years = 6, n_origins = 5, n_draws = 50,
                          method = "errors"), x)
fe$calibration
#>    horizon origins cells    mean_error tuning coverage
#>      <int>   <num> <int>         <num>  <num>    <num>
#> 1:       1       5   142 -0.0061264434      1        1
#> 2:       2       5   142 -0.0052819251      1        1
#> 3:       3       4   142 -0.0044615082      1        1
#> 4:       4       3   142 -0.0029353580      1        1
#> 5:       5       2   142  0.0003896597      1        1
fce <- mt_forecast(fe, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
